metadata.title: The essence of creative thinking in PISA 2022: An item-level machine learning approach to construct validity at the facet level

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study reanalyzed PISA 2022 microdata and restricted the analytic sample to students who completed the creative thinking assessment (142,564 students across 63 countries/economies). For preprocessing, the authors explicitly excluded sampling weights from the merged dataset to reduce noise and file size, and they removed PVs for creative thinking while retaining single-item scores and process indicators. The paper does not report applying complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures; instead, it fits random-forest models using the ranger engine in R. Because the models are standard ML classifiers that do not natively incorporate PISA complex-survey weights, the weighting strategy is effectively omitted, which may leave some clustering/unequal selection effects only partially addressed by the original PISA design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses one randomly selected plausible value per cognitive competence domain (mathematics, reading, science) as predictors, but it does not describe how missing values in questionnaire/process variables were handled prior to model fitting. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain non-trivial missingness in background and process indicators, and the choice between listwise deletion, imputation, or model-based handling can affect variable importance and predicted score probabilities. The authors also do not specify whether any missingness was addressed within the long-format item–person restructuring step.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Reanalyzed PISA 2022 and restricted the analytic sample to students who completed the creative thinking assessment. Removed sampling weights and excluded creative-thinking plausible values, retaining raw item scores (scored via a three-step partial credit system) plus process indicators (e.g., response time, latency to first action, number of actions, revisits/short visits). Restructured data into long format (one row per item–person combination) and split the dataset into three facet-specific datasets (GDI, GCI, EII), adding student-level mean values of scores/process items from the other facets as predictors. For robustness, repeated analyses using a second randomly selected set of plausible values for the cognitive competence domains.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (15-year-olds) — facet generate diverse ideas (GDI) item-level
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking item score categories (GDI; no/partial/full credit)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — accuracy: 67.5% (permutation variable importance used; no additional discrimination metrics reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking the study leveraged item characteristics (item identifier/domain), student characteristics (e.g., gender/grade), behavioral engagement indicators (e.g., total time on task, latency, number of actions), and general academic competence (reading/mathematics/science PVs) to predict creative thinking item score categories for the GDI facet, finding that engagement and general academic competence plus socio-economic background were among the strongest predictors and that item/domain effects were central. This indicates that PISA’s GDI item scores may reflect broader diligence and general reasoning resources as much as ideational fluency, so facet-level reporting should be interpreted with construct-confounding caution.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (15-year-olds) — facet generate creative ideas (GCI) item-level
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking item score categories (GCI; no/partial/full credit)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — accuracy: 64.5% (permutation variable importance used; no additional discrimination metrics reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking the study leveraged item characteristics (item identifier/domain), socio-economic indicators (e.g., home possessions and parents’ education), behavioral engagement indicators, and general academic competence PVs to predict creative thinking item score categories for the GCI facet, finding that the influential predictor profile was highly similar to the other facets and that engagement/competence dominated over creativity self-report measures. This indicates that the GCI facet may not be empirically separable from general academic and motivational resources in PISA, suggesting that composite or facet interpretations should be validated further before using them for fine-grained construct claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (15-year-olds) — facet evaluate and improve ideas (EII) item-level
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking item score categories (EII; no/partial/full credit)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — accuracy: 65.8% (permutation variable importance used; no additional discrimination metrics reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking the study leveraged item characteristics, socio-economic background, behavioral engagement indicators, and general academic competence PVs to predict creative thinking item score categories for the EII facet, finding that predicted score probabilities differed by content domain and that higher competence generally increased the likelihood of partial/full credit while the facet-specific predictor profiles remained remarkably similar across GDI/GCI/EII. This indicates that EII scores may be driven by general reasoning and engagement rather than a distinct convergent-evaluation process alone, so policy use of facet scores should avoid assuming they isolate different cognitive mechanisms.

data.outcome_summary: This study reanalyzed PISA 2022 creative thinking item-level data for 15-year-olds, restricting to students who completed the creative thinking assessment (142,564 students across 63 countries/economies) and predicting three facet-specific item score categories (no/partial/full credit) using random forests. The authors did not use the official creative-thinking composite proficiency PVs; instead, they used raw item scores and retained process indicators (e.g., total time on task, latency to first action, number of actions). For the three facet models, predictive accuracy was 67.5% (GDI), 64.5% (GCI), and 65.8% (EII), with permutation variable importance showing that behavioral engagement, general academic competence (reading/mathematics/science PVs), and socio-economic background were among the strongest predictors. Explainability via permutation importance and ALE plots indicated domain-specific probability patterns and only subtle competence-by-domain interactions. Limitations include omission of sampling weights and the use of one randomly selected PV per competence domain, so results reflect predictive associations rather than causal construct validation.
